title: Week 34 Quiz — Globalization, Trade, Development, and Migration

questions.prompt: Which term best matches this definition: Increasing cross-border connection in production, finance, information, culture, and movement.
questions.explanation: Globalization is the course term defined as: Increasing cross-border connection in production, finance, information, culture, and movement.

questions.prompt: Which term best matches this definition: The linked stages through which a good or service is designed, produced, transported, and sold.
questions.explanation: Supply Chain is the course term defined as: The linked stages through which a good or service is designed, produced, transported, and sold.

questions.prompt: Which term best matches this definition: The ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another producer.
questions.explanation: Comparative Advantage is the course term defined as: The ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another producer.

questions.prompt: Which term best matches this definition: A measure used to describe economic or social conditions.
questions.explanation: Development Indicator is the course term defined as: A measure used to describe economic or social conditions.

questions.prompt: Which term best matches this definition: Money sent by migrants to people in another place, often family members.
questions.explanation: Remittance is the course term defined as: Money sent by migrants to people in another place, often family members.

questions.prompt: A low-cost product creates jobs in one country but depends on hazardous labor and long-distance shipping. Which evaluation is strongest?
choices: Low price proves the supply chain is beneficial overall.
Any global supply chain is harmful by definition.
Evaluate price, employment, labor conditions, environmental costs, resilience, ownership, and who bears each risk or benefit.
questions.explanation: Global production can create gains and shift costs; evaluation requires tracing benefits, risks, and distribution across the chain.

questions.prompt: Why might two countries reverse places in a development ranking when the indicator changes from income to life expectancy?
choices: Different indicators measure different dimensions of well-being, so no single ranking captures development completely.
Development rankings are fraudulent whenever they change.
Life expectancy is unrelated to development.
Income and health always move together.
questions.explanation: Income, health, education, inequality, rights, resilience, and environment capture different dimensions of development.

questions.prompt: A family migrates because of employment, relatives abroad, drought, and a new visa rule. What does the case demonstrate?
choices: Migration always has one dominant cause.
Migration can result from interacting economic, family, environmental, policy, network, and individual factors.
Climate is the only meaningful cause of migration.
questions.explanation: Migration decisions often combine structural pressures, networks, policy constraints, and individual agency.

questions.prompt: Students trace a phone from minerals through assembly, shipping, retail, disposal, and recycling. Which evidence set is strongest?
choices: A single advertisement from the retailer.
At least four source types covering materials, labor, transport/ownership, and environmental or end-of-life impacts.
Only a map of the final retail market.
questions.explanation: A global-product investigation is strongest when it corroborates multiple stages and dimensions of the supply chain.

questions.prompt: Emissions are shown as national totals, per-person values, and values per unit of output. Why should students compare all three?
choices: Only the largest national total is meaningful.
Using more than one measure makes comparison impossible.
Changing denominators can reveal different questions about scale, individual burden, and production efficiency.
questions.explanation: Totals and normalized measures answer different questions; responsible quantitative reasoning makes the denominator explicit.

shortResponse.prompt: Using at least two specific pieces of evidence, answer: How should societies evaluate the gains, risks, and unequal effects of global interdependence?
shortResponse.exemplar: A full-credit response states a defensible answer to the essential question, uses two accurate details from the week, explains how each detail supports the claim, and acknowledges one complexity or limitation.
